paras: The Houston Emancipation Day shooting took place before daylight on June 20, 1882, at the grounds where Black residents of Houston, Texas, were celebrating emancipation. Charles F. Witham, a white printer, was shot dead, Deputy Marshal Wm. Glass was wounded, and a Black man was killed and two Black people wounded by what the dispatches called stray shots. Several Black men were arrested, and three were later charged with Witham's murder.

Houston's Black community held its emancipation celebration on grounds of its own, and according to the Lake Charles Echo the gathering heard a speech from E. J. Davis, a former Republican governor of Texas. Witham was a member of the Typographical Union and treasurer of the Houston lodge of Young Native Houstonians.

A Houston dispatch printed in Texas papers described a "fatal row" just before daylight in which four shots, fired "as in a volley," passed through Witham's body and head and killed him instantly. Glass was shot as he stooped to lift the body, the ball entering behind his shoulder and coming out at his neck, and he was expected to recover. John Glass, the deputy's brother, went to his aid but was disarmed and put off the grounds.

A Black man named Harry Nelson (Harris Nelson in the Austin paper) was killed, "it is supposed by a stray shot," while Frank H. Spencer and an unnamed Black woman were wounded by shots from the celebrants. The same dispatch said several white men had been ejected from the grounds and that fear among Black residents ended the rest of the celebration.

On the day of the shooting police arrested two Black men, Bufford for wounding Glass and Johnson for shooting Witham, according to a Dallas Herald special. The national wire instead named Ed. Jamison, called "a notorious negro politician," as one of Witham's killers, along with Frank Bufford. By October, John Helm, known as "Nosey John," was in jail under indictment for the murder, and the case of Ed Jameson, Frank Buford and John Helm was set for trial on October 24. No report of an inquest or of the trial's outcome was found.

Texas papers carried the Houston dispatch under headlines such as "Bloody Termination of Emancipation Day" in San Antonio and "Sad Ending of Emancipation Day" in Austin, presenting the white victims' side as fact. A shorter wire version ran on June 22 in papers from New York to St. Paul, where the Daily Globe headed it "Stray Bullets Promiscuous," while the Savannah Morning News titled it "A Fatal Negro Fusilade"; a one-sentence "scrimmage" item reached Nevada two days later. A condensed Arkansas brief garbled the story, making Witham a deputy marshal and naming the Black dead man Henderson.

The Lake Charles Echo in Louisiana went further, calling the killing a "cold-blooded murder" committed for no reason but Witham's visit to the grounds and treating it as typical of the "natural instincts" of the race. The Echo set the shooting against Davis's praise of the celebrants' progress and hoped "a speedy retribution" would be meted out to the men arrested. None of the coverage gave an account from the celebrants or explained why white men had been ejected from the grounds.

Accounts differ on the Black man killed, named Harry or Harris Nelson in the Texas dispatch, left unnamed as a "colored boy" in the wire, and called Henderson in the Arkansas brief, which alone also lists a W. Myers shot in the hand. The Texas dispatch, the fullest and earliest report, is the better evidence on these points.

reader.title: Houston Emancipation Day shooting
bases: Every account describes a shooting at a Black Emancipation Day celebration in which, by the white press's account, Black celebrants shot a white man dead and wounded a white deputy, while a Black man was killed and others wounded by what the dispatches called stray shots (A1, A4, A5).

Separate Texas specials (A1/A4, A2) and the national wire (A5) agree on Witham's death, Glass's wounding and a Black death at the emancipation grounds, and later Houston news confirms indictments (A19, A20).

accounts.label: Houston dispatch (Texas papers)
accounts.gist: In a 'fatal row' before daybreak the Black celebrants killed Witham with a volley and wounded Glass; a Black man was killed and two Black people wounded by stray shots, and white men were ejected from the grounds.

accounts.label: National wire
accounts.gist: Witham was fired upon by 'negroes' (or 'a negro') and killed, Glass shot lifting the body, a 'colored boy' killed by a stray bullet, and Jamison and Bufford arrested.

accounts.label: Lake Charles Echo editorial
accounts.gist: The celebrants committed a 'cold-blooded murder' of Witham for no reason except that he visited the grounds with Glass and others, after a speech by E. J. Davis.

framing.detail: Texas papers ran the dispatch as 'Bloody Termination of Emancipation Day' and 'Sad Ending of Emancipation Day', placing the blame on 'the negroes' without any account from the celebrants.
Northern, western and southern papers carried a short wire item, headed 'Shooting in Texas', 'Stray Bullets Promiscuous' and 'A Fatal Negro Fusilade', calling Jamison 'a notorious negro politician'.
The Lake Charles Echo turned the killing into an attack on the race and on Reconstruction politics, hoping 'a speedy retribution may be meted out' to the arrested men.

conflicts.note: The Texas dispatch (A1, A4) is the fullest and closest source; the Henderson name appears only in a late, condensed Arkansas brief that also garbles Witham's role.
